subject: Art & Design
title: The Exposure Triangle Explained
description: Learn The Exposure Triangle Explained in one minute.

hook.text: Aperture, shutter speed, and ISO. Change one, and you must adjust another to keep the exposure right.

buildup.text: Aperture controls how much light enters. Shutter speed controls how long. ISO controls sensor sensitivity.

discovery.text: They're a triangle: widening aperture brightens the image but blurs backgrounds. There's always a tradeoff.

twist.text: High ISO brightens dark scenes but adds grain (noise). The 'free brightness' comes at a quality cost.

climax.text: Mastering the triangle means choosing which tradeoff serves the image — blur, motion, or noise.

punchline.text: There's no 'correct' exposure. Only the exposure your story needs.

quiz.question: What are the three elements of the exposure triangle?

details.summary: The exposure triangle balances three settings — aperture (light entering the lens), shutter speed (duration of exposure), and ISO (sensor sensitivity) — to achieve correct brightness.
details.whyItMatters: Understanding the exposure triangle is the gateway to creative control in photography. Without it, you rely on automatic modes. With it, you can intentionally create the depth of field, motion effects, and image quality you envision.
takeaways: Aperture, shutter speed, and ISO balance to control exposure
Changing one requires compensating with another
Each setting has creative side effects beyond brightness

faq.question: Which setting should you adjust first?
faq.answer: Start with the setting most important to your creative intent. If depth of field matters most, set aperture first. If freezing or blurring motion matters, set shutter speed first. Then adjust the remaining settings to achieve correct exposure. ISO is typically the last adjustment.

faq.question: What is ISO and why does higher ISO add noise?
faq.answer: ISO amplifies the sensor's electrical signal. Higher amplification brightens the image but also amplifies random electronic interference (noise), creating grainy, speckled images. Modern cameras handle high ISO much better than older ones, but lower ISO always produces cleaner images.
